blindSummary:
A 2024 conversion-practices ban (bipartisan, in force 4 April 2025) makes practices directed at changing or suppressing sexual orientation or gender identity criminal offences punishable by up to five years' imprisonment, including taking a person interstate or overseas for that purpose or engaging a provider from outside this state/province. A civil complaints scheme runs through the state's anti-discrimination body. This state/province also operates an explicit self-identification prison-placement policy, reducing the risk of inappropriate custody for a detained gender-nonconforming visitor.

Against these strong legal protections, this state/province carries a concentrated violence pattern. A trans woman was killed in her apartment (January 2020); the accused admitted killing her after learning she was transgender, and the case went to murder trial at the state's supreme court — a positive institutional response. A 25-year-old foreign trans woman who had arrived in the country approximately six weeks earlier was strangled; her killer received only 22 months on a consensual-strangulation account that broadcaster reporting showed the court never heard contested. Two killings of trans women in the same state/province within roughly a year, with one adequate and one clearly inadequate sentencing outcome, is recorded as a pattern plus a contested institutional response, not as isolated incidents. This state/province is a common-law jurisdiction with no statutory bill of rights and no anti-vilification offence of this kind.

The criminal conversion-practice ban and self-identification custody rule are real protections, though narrow in direct visitor exposure (a typical tourist is unlikely to encounter a conversion-practice provider). The violence-and-sentencing pattern is more relevant to a visitor's physical safety and shows both institutional capability (the murder trial) and institutional failure (the 22-month sentence).
blindSourceSummaries: State government ministerial release (4 April 2025): the 2024 conversion-practices ban commenced, making conversion and suppression practices toward LGBTQ+ people (psychological or medical interventions, counselling, or sustained pressure to change or suppress sexual orientation or gender identity) a crime punishable up to five years' imprisonment, with taking a person out of this state/province for the purpose carrying up to three years; a civil complaints scheme runs through the state's anti-discrimination body with referral to the civil tribunal; carve-outs preserve general religious teaching and parental discussion; the release also notes the premier's apology over historical gay convictions and government support for all 19 recommendations of a special commission of inquiry into LGBTQ hate crimes.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (the official legislation site blocks automated fetches); the underlying record is the 2024 conversion-practices ban (in force 4 April 2025) as cited by the government release - the criminal and civil text the release summarises.

A queer news outlet's report on state supreme court proceedings over the killing of a trans woman found dead in her apartment in January 2020 (aged 69): the accused, a foreign student, admitted assaulting and unlawfully killing her after learning she was transgender but pleaded not guilty to murder; the prosecution rejected his manslaughter plea, sending the matter to a murder trial.

A national broadcaster's long-form investigation (2 July 2021) into the killing of a 25-year-old foreign trans woman strangled in regional areas of this state/province about six weeks after arriving in the country: her killer pleaded guilty to strangulation in what he claimed was consensual sexual choking gone wrong and received only 22 months without trial; evidence never tested in court (a disturbing final video call, ambulance logs, first-responder statement, medical records, autopsy) was reviewed by a senior retired judge, who said a miscarriage of justice may have occurred and described the case as far more serious manslaughter than the sentencing judge recognised.
